passage:
It was the first Diwali since Amma's two long years of cancer had ended, and Jahnavi had signed up for the hospice festival shift so she wouldn't have to sit at home. At seven the power went out across the ward. In the dark, she and Disha, the volunteer coordinator, went bed to bed lighting battery diyas and reading out patients' messages from their phones. Jahnavi knew how to plump a pillow without jolting anyone; she had learned on Amma.
An old man squeezed her hand. "You're good at this."
"I had practice," she said, smiling.
Later, packing up, she found herself crying in the supply room. Disha sat down beside her. "Helping them doesn't mean you stop missing her. Take tomorrow off."
Jahnavi nodded and, for once, didn't argue.

qa.q: What happened at seven during the Diwali shift?
qa.a: The power went out across the ward.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi sign up for the Diwali shift?
qa.a: She did not want to sit at home grieving on the first Diwali without Amma, and caring for patients turned the loss into a sense of purpose.

qa.q: What did Disha suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Taking the next day off, because caring work can give meaning, but grief for Amma still needs its own time and space.

qa.q: How does the old man experience Jahnavi's care?
qa.a: He feels comforted by her gentle skill, squeezing her hand and telling her she is good at this.

grounding: A young adult who lost her mother to a long illness volunteers at a hospice, finding purpose while her grief still needs room.

On Children's Day, Ma'am picked me to read the story aloud. I got to "magnificent" and it came out "mag-nif-nif-icent". My face went hot. So I crossed my eyes, stuck out my tongue and said, "Sonali has broken down, please restart." Everyone laughed, even Ma'am. Avni laughed so hard she snorted.
It felt good, like I was in charge again. But at lunch my tummy still felt tight.
I do the funny face a lot now. When I don't know an answer. When I'm scared to read. Sometimes I wish I could just say, "That word is hard for me."

qa.q: Which word did Sonali stumble on?
qa.a: "Magnificent".

qa.q: Why did Sonali make a silly face?
qa.a: Sonali felt embarrassed and hot-faced 😅, and getting everyone to laugh along felt like being in charge again instead of being laughed at.

qa.q: What could help Sonali in future?
qa.a: Quietly telling the teacher or a friend that some words are hard, and practising reading aloud at home, so the funny face is not needed every time.

qa.q: How does Avni see the moment?
qa.a: Avni just finds it hilarious, snorting with laughter, and probably does not notice Sonali's tight tummy or worry.

grounding: A child who stumbles while reading aloud clowns to get the class laughing, while the joking hides worry.

passage:
Devika, sit, your laptop will survive. Let me tell you about my final-year project. There were four of us: me, Sarika, the serious one, plus Farhan, Meenal and Joel. We built a little water-sensor robot. The night before the demo, in full monsoon, the lab roof leaked right onto it. Fizz, smoke, dead.
We stood there dripping, and Farhan said, "Well. It detected water." I started laughing, and then all four of us were laughing so hard the watchman came to check. It didn't fix anything. But after five minutes we could breathe.
Then Meenal grabbed the whiteboard marker. "What can we show by ten tomorrow?" We rebuilt the circuit on a breadboard and demoed with a bucket. We got a B. Honestly, the best B of my life.

qa.q: What happened to the robot the night before the demo?
qa.a: The lab roof leaked right onto it, and it fizzed, smoked and died.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when the laughing started?
qa.a: Sarika was shocked and hurt by the loss, and Farhan's absurd joke let the group feel amused and breathe instead of despairing.

qa.q: What turning point moved the group from laughing to working?
qa.a: Meenal grabbing the marker and asking what they could show by ten; the laughter gave them distance, and the question started the planning.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt after making the joke?
qa.a: Farhan probably felt relieved that the joke broke the tension and pulled everyone together rather than seeming unkind.

grounding: A group of students laugh at the absurdity of a ruined project, then use the relief to plan and rebuild.

passage:
You remind me of Kalyani, you know, beta. When I was about your age, twenty-four and working in Pune, Kalyani was the funniest one in our group. Every dinner she had us crying with laughter.
But I began to notice something. If anyone asked, "How's your mother's health?" or "Are you okay after the transfer?", she'd pull a face and say, "Next question, Anjali, the court is adjourned!" Everyone laughed. Every time.
One night, after the others left, she went quiet, staring at her phone. The jokes just stopped. So I didn't ask in front of anyone. I walked her to the bus stop and said, "You make us all laugh so much. Who makes you feel okay?"
She didn't answer that night. Two days later she called me, and we talked for three hours about her mother.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say when asked a serious question?
qa.a: "Next question, Anjali, the court is adjourned!"

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as the pattern became clear?
qa.a: Anjali felt curious and quietly concerned, sensing that the constant jokes were covering something painful.

qa.q: What choice did Anjali make at the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Anjali waited until the jokes stopped and asked privately at the bus stop, without an audience, which gave Kalyani room to open up two days later.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Kalyani inside the laughing group?
qa.a: She may have felt lonely and worried about her mother, using jokes to dodge questions she was not ready to answer in front of everyone.

grounding: A friend notices that the funniest person in the group dodges every serious question with a joke, and checks in privately when the joking stops.

passage:
It was New Year's Eve, and I thought a fresh year was a good moment. We were sticking glow stars on the balcony ceiling when I said, "Zubin, can we look at the credit card bill together this week?"
He grinned. "Money is a social construct, darling."
I laughed; he's genuinely funny. I tried again at midnight, after the fireworks. "I mean it. I'm worried about the card."
"Worried? On New Year? That's illegal." People on the next balcony laughed. I didn't. Looking back, that was when I felt most alone that night, surrounded by laughter.
On the second of January, I, Shreya, wrote it down plainly and handed Zubin the note: "I need one hour, no jokes, this Sunday." He read it twice and, for once, nodded without a punchline.

qa.q: What were Shreya and Zubin doing when Shreya first raised the bill?
qa.a: Sticking glow stars on the balcony ceiling.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when the neighbours laughed at Zubin's joke?
qa.a: Shreya felt dismissed and alone, because the humour kept blocking a worry that needed attention.

qa.q: What worked in the end, and why?
qa.a: Writing the request plainly and asking for one hour with no jokes made the topic hard to deflect, while still leaving room for Zubin to agree.

qa.q: Why might Zubin keep joking about money?
qa.a: Zubin may feel uneasy or embarrassed about the card, and jokes let him avoid a topic that makes him uncomfortable.

grounding: Someone trying to talk about a credit card bill keeps getting witty deflections and feels dismissed until the request is made plainly.

passage:
Last week Avni was, in Ira's words, "literally the best human alive". She had shared her notes, stayed on the phone all through the storm and remembered Ira's cat's birthday.
Then came Holi. The colony ground was packed and deafening with dhol and water pistols, and Avni went off with the girls from her tuition for twenty minutes. When Ira finally found her, she was drenched in green, laughing with them. Ira turned away.
That evening Ira texted her cousin: "Avni is a total traitor. She never actually cared. Fake from day one."
Her cousin replied, "Is this the same Avni who stayed on the phone with you through the whole storm?"
Ira stared at the message, face still pink with gulal, and didn't reply.

qa.q: How long did Avni go off with the girls from her tuition?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Ira suddenly call Avni a total traitor?
qa.a: Ira felt hurt and left out 😢, and in that strong disappointment it was hard to hold Avni's good side and the small slight together.

qa.q: What could Ira try before deciding about the friendship?
qa.a: Wait for the feeling to cool, remember the shared notes and the storm call, and tell Avni simply that she felt left out at Holi.

qa.q: How might Avni see the day?
qa.a: She probably thought she was just playing Holi for a while, and would be confused and hurt to learn Ira now sees her as a traitor.

grounding: A teenager who called her friend perfect a week ago calls her a traitor after a small slight at Holi.

passage:
Ramzan, 14th night. Hostel.
Can't sleep, so writing. Two weeks ago I called Dr Zainab "the reason I'm in this course". I kept her lecture notes in a special file. I stayed after iftar just to ask her questions.
Today she handed back my draft and said, in front of the whole seminar, "Ayesha, this is sloppy. You can do far better." That's it. One line.
And now I can't stand her. She's arrogant. Her lectures are recycled. Honestly, she probably never liked me.
Okay, written down, that sounds extreme. Last week she was perfect and today she's the worst person on campus? Both can't be true. Maybe she's a good teacher who had a sharp moment, and my draft really was rushed.
Still angry. Going to sleep on it.

qa.q: What did Dr Zainab say about the draft?
qa.a: "Ayesha, this is sloppy. You can do far better."

qa.q: Why did Ayesha suddenly decide Dr Zainab was arrogant?
qa.a: Ayesha felt humiliated and resentful after the public comment, and because Dr Zainab had been on such a high pedestal, one flaw made her seem all bad.

qa.q: What could Ayesha do next?
qa.a: Sleep on it, reread the draft for the rushed parts, and perhaps ask Dr Zainab what "far better" would look like.

qa.q: How might Dr Zainab have meant the comment?
qa.a: She may have been frustrated but also showing belief in Ayesha, since she said Ayesha could do far better.

grounding: A student who idolised a professor turns bitter after one harsh remark, then starts to question the swing.

passage:
During Semana Santa in Seville the streets were jammed with processions, and Esther's phone was buried in her bag while she helped her aunt carry chairs. For months Ines had called her "the only person who actually gets me".
When Esther checked her phone at eleven, there were nine missed calls and a message: "I just needed to rant about the exam and you vanished. Knew it. You're useless like everyone else."
Esther sat on the church steps, bewildered. She typed three angry replies and deleted them all. Then she wrote: "I'm sorry I missed your calls. I was helping my aunt and didn't hear. I care about you, and I'm not okay with being called useless. I can talk tomorrow at ten if you want."
She put the phone away and went back to the chairs.

qa.q: How many missed calls did Esther find?
qa.a: Nine missed calls.

qa.q: What was Esther feeling on the church steps?
qa.a: Esther felt bewildered and stung, going from "the only person who gets me" to "useless" in one evening, and angry enough to draft three replies.

qa.q: Which part of Esther's reply keeps a steady boundary?
qa.a: She apologises for the missed calls and says she cares, but states clearly she is not okay being called useless and offers a set time to talk, without insulting back.

qa.q: What might Ines have been feeling when sending that message?
qa.a: Ines was probably upset about the exam and felt abandoned when the calls went unanswered, so the disappointment flipped into seeing Esther as all bad.

grounding: A friend once praised as the only one who understands is called useless after missed calls, and replies with care and a firm boundary.

passage:
Subject: Following up on today

Hi Sonali,
Thanks for coming to talk to me after the stand-up. I could hear how frustrated you are, and I want to take it seriously.
I've noticed that over the last few weeks, colleagues have swung quickly between "amazing" and "impossible" for you. Last month Mohan was "the only one who pulls his weight"; today he "sabotaged" the launch. I'm not saying your feelings aren't real. I just can't be fair to anyone, you included, without specifics.
Could you jot down exactly what happened on Tuesday: what was said, what was missed, and when? I'll ask Mohan for his account too, and then the three of us can sort out the handover.
You're a strong analyst, and I want this to work for everyone.
Vandana

qa.q: What did Sonali say about Mohan last month?
qa.a: That he was "the only one who pulls his weight".

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling while writing the email?
qa.a: Vandana felt concerned and careful: sympathetic to Sonali's frustration but uneasy about the swings between "amazing" and "impossible".

qa.q: Why is asking for specifics a wise step?
qa.a: Details of what was said and missed let Vandana judge fairly, hear Mohan too, and move from heroes and villains to fixing the handover 👍.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel reading the email?
qa.a: Sonali might feel heard and a little challenged, perhaps defensive at the pattern being named but reassured by the praise and the fair process.

grounding: A manager notices a team member sorting colleagues into heroes and villains and asks for specifics while staying fair to all.
